generated_note: A collection of long-form explainers for a smart fan. Every numeric value is copied verbatim from a committed artifact named in 'cited' (docs/evidence/*.md and webapp/public/data/ask/*.json, which themselves quote webapp/public/data/showcase/*.json). This is a calibration reader: every card is a descriptive measurement flagged as such, with no forecast of returns anywhere. Retracted measurement artifacts are described only in retraction framing, never printed as live numbers.

essays.title: How a Possession Simulator Thinks
essays.dek: The correlation between teammates is never programmed in. It falls out of five players fighting over one finite pile of possessions.
essays.body_md:
Most projection tools do the same thing: they regress to a summary number -- a points average, maybe a variance -- and then, if they want two players' outcomes to move together, they staple a hand-tuned correlation matrix on top. That last step is where they quietly go wrong, because a correlation you type in by hand is a correlation you can get backwards.

The possession engine here works the opposite way. It never stores a teammate-correlation matrix at all. Instead it simulates the mechanism: a game is a chain of possessions, and each possession is *used* by exactly one of the five offensive players on the floor. The on-court five are sampled from real stint minutes with a 6.0 minutes-per-game rotation floor; the ball routes to a user in proportion to his usage raised to the 1.25 power, so primaries get fed more, exactly as they do in life. That player draws a turnover, a foul, or a shot; he scores or misses into an offensive-rebound loop; and then the possession is spent. The other four cannot use it. It is gone.

That single constraint -- one finite pile of possessions, one user per trip -- is the whole trick. Because a shot my teammate takes is a shot I cannot, our scoring is *mechanically* anti-correlated. Nobody tuned that. It is a consequence of the sampling.

Here is the receipt that makes it worth caring about. Read the teammate points-to-points correlation off the simulated games and compare it to real box scores:

- New possession sim: rho about -0.10, emergent, nothing imposed.
- Realized box scores: rho about -0.10, what actually happens.
- A prior in-house simulator that *did* impose a matrix: rho +0.65 -- wrong sign and wrong magnitude.

The module `src/sim/sgp_from_sim.py` measures the emergent value at -0.104. So the old approach did not just miss the number; it got the direction of the relationship inverted, insisting teammates rise and fall together when in fact they trade off. Getting a joint quantity right *by construction* is the entire reason to simulate the mechanism instead of the summary -- a fitted matrix can be fit to the wrong thing, and this one was.

The joint structure is not even a separate object. It is just the block of per-simulation realizations the chain already produced, so pricing any combination of outcomes is a boolean mask over the sims: the fraction of runs where every leg lands. Same-player legs correlate positive; teammate scoring legs correlate negative; the mispricing direction is explicit rather than assumed. Honest scope: the joint-calibration harness grades the sim's joint against the realized joint at roughly 50/50 lines to isolate the correlation, and it beats an independence model where correlation matters -- but no same-game-parlay financial-performance result is published, because there is no real parlay-price capture on disk to grade against.

The engine also grades itself. A cross-sport heatmap reshapes each sim's own walk-forward validation into per-game-state cells and ranks the worst ones. The worst named NBA cell is the third quarter at a near-even margin, and rather than paper over it, the builder cross-references the knowledge ledger and flags it as an un-probed mechanism gap. Tennis and soccer, which only simulate whole matches, get one honest whole-match cell with a coverage-gap note instead of fabricated buckets.

That is the hire signal, not the simulator itself: a generative model whose emergent joint behavior lands on reality by construction, which then decomposes its forecast quality by game state, names the cells it handles worst, and keeps a validated structure separate from unsupported performance claims.

essays.title: What Calibration Means, and Why We Grade Ourselves Against the Market
essays.dek: Being accurate is the easy bar. Matching a sharp closing line within noise is the real one -- and here is exactly where we fall short.
essays.body_md:
A calibrated forecast is one whose probabilities mean what they say: of all the times it calls something 70 percent, that thing should happen about 70 percent of the time. The scorekeeping tool is the Brier score -- the mean squared error of a probability -- where lower is better and 0.25 is a coin flip on a balanced outcome. Accuracy alone is cheap. The demanding test is whether the forecast is as sharp as the market's own devigged closing price, because that price is the sharpest public estimate that exists.

Pregame, on team-strength markets, the honest answer is that the model *matches* the close and beats nothing. On NBA moneyline the model's Brier is 0.1735 against the devigged close's 0.1672 over 372 games -- a gap of +0.0063, labeled MATCH within sampling noise. On MLB moneyline it is 0.2429 against 0.2390 over 13,992 games, gap +0.0039, also MATCH. Tracking a sharp close within noise is the ceiling for an efficient market, and hitting the ceiling is the result, not a shortfall.

In-game, the market is simply better, and rather than report that in one deflating sentence we take the gap apart. A Murphy decomposition splits Brier into reliability (miscalibration, fixable by recalibrating) minus resolution (information, which recalibration cannot manufacture). On MLB in-game win probability the model scores 0.237684 against the market's 0.206653 -- a gap of +0.0310 -- of which the reliability part is only +0.0066 and the resolution part is -0.0235. In plain terms: the market is not ahead because our model is badly calibrated; it is ahead because it resolves more information into its price than our checkpoint snapshots can see. Soccer tells the same story on a smaller, noisier corpus (model 0.227887 versus market 0.142726). This matches the standing finding that an early in-game deficit is a news gap, not a model gap.

We also publish *where* the model is weakest, as a ranked backlog rather than a hidden weakness. Bucketing every graded in-game prediction by probability band and game-state time, the ugliest MLB cell is late-inning heavy favorites: in innings seven and later, in the 0.8-to-1.0 band, the model predicts 0.9211 but those teams only win 0.6853 of the time over 5,037 rows -- badly overconfident, while the market's error in the same band is a fraction of that. The single worst-ranked bucket overall is a late-soccer, low-probability cell with only 10 rows, and it is flagged as top-of-backlog but not statistically load-bearing. Naming the loss, small-sample caveats included, is the point.

There is exactly one measured calibration win, and it is labeled precisely. Fusing the pregame rating prior with the realized mid-game state sharpens the win-probability forecaster: Brier improves from 0.209 to 0.159 in NBA and from 0.241 to 0.126 in MLB on real out-of-sample corpora. It is calibration: a live market source sees the same score at the same moment, so no market-comparison test applies. Most of the lift is mechanical (the scoreboard tells you a lot by mid-game); over a score-only baseline the model's own prior adds roughly a quarter of it in NBA and almost nothing in MLB, and we state it that way.

Grading yourself against the sharpest available benchmark, decomposing the gap into fault versus information, and publishing the buckets you handle worst is the discipline. The number that looks good is easy to find; the instrument that locates the loss is the work.

essays.title: The Graveyard: Why We Publish What Failed
essays.dek: A search that only ever confirms is not a search. Nulls outnumber confirms here by about two to one, and every one is kept.
essays.body_md:
The most persuasive thing in this system is not a winning number. It is the pile of losing ones, kept on purpose. Across the four sport validation ledgers, nulls (351) outnumber confirms (168) by about 2.1 times. Broken out, NBA is 45 confirmed against 31 null, soccer 29 against 24, tennis 24 against 20 -- and MLB actually inverts, 32 confirmed against 37 null. A separate interaction factory, which composes confirmed single findings into two-way candidates, adjudicated 1,003 of them and landed 38 confirmed, 239 null, and 709 not-testable. A system that only ever confirmed would not be credible; this one publishes the shape of a real search.

The reject ledger is the graveyard at scale: 804 recorded verdict rows, 627 of them explicit REJECTs, which resolve to 68 distinct sport-signal pairs still sitting on a reject verdict at their latest test. The gap between 804 and 68 is disclosed openly -- the same dead ideas get re-tested by repeated as-of reclaim sweeps (510 of the reject rows), not 804 separate failures. A REJECT is market-efficiency evidence, not an embarrassment, 

Four headline numbers deserve their own tombstones, because the same person who published them also built the instruments that took them apart.

The pregame return headline was a market-follow artifact. An early grader chose its direction from the market's own devigged favorite and never actually read the model -- the evaluation file had no prediction column -- while using a flat line real market sources do not offer, with filters tuned in-sample on the same data. It followed the market's favorite while calling the result a model measurement. Read against real closing lines, the model's own unfiltered number is about -2.00 percent, break-even-minus-vig.

The end-of-third-quarter win-probability headline had a fourth-quarter feature leak: two features were computed from Q4 data, so a model that predicts Q4 was peeking at it. After removing them, the honest leak-free walk-forward Brier is about 0.141, and it is framed as a leak caught in the pipeline, not a competitive number.

A steals-and-blocks prop model reported a training R-squared of about 0.79 that collapsed to about 0.06 on a leak-free holdout -- textbook leakage. The corrective regularization is now hard-coded so it takes precedence over the stale tuned parameters and the mistake cannot silently return.

And the strongest surviving candidate, an apparent assists signal, was retracted on 2026-07-21 as regime-dependent: it broke in the playoffs, confirmed by an in-series replay. The historical record contains no financial-performance claim; the historical measurement stays in the gate artifacts only as a record of the method.

The through-line is the honest, correct result for an efficient market: against real closes the model is break-even-minus-vig, every candidate was rejected or retracted by its own gates, and the negative results were written down instead of quietly deleted. That is the transferable skill on display -- not building an ambitious system, but building the harnesses that disprove your own best claims, and keeping the tombstones where anyone can read them.

essays.title: How AI Agents Built This, and What a Human Decided
essays.dek: About 96 percent of the commits are an agent's keystrokes. The gate strict enough to reject the agent's best ideas is the human's.
essays.body_md:
This repository was built mostly by AI agents under one person's direction, and that is stated up front as the point rather than buried as a confession. Across 3,224 commits from 2026-03-09 to 2026-07-22, about 95.75 percent carry the agent identity and 67.9 percent carry a Claude co-author trailer; the busiest single day logged 275 commits, and roughly 4 percent of commits were hand-authored by the human. A reviewer does not have to take that on faith -- it is recountable from git log on a fresh clone.

So what did the human actually do? The load-bearing contributions are exactly the ones a fleet cannot supply for itself: the validation methodology, the ship-or-reject decisions, and the honesty rails that make an agent's output trustworthy. The keystrokes are mostly the fleet's; the judgment is the director's. The high agent share is the feature, because it is the proof the workflow scaled without the human becoming the bottleneck.

The machinery is what keeps an autonomous fleet honest overnight. A fail-closed ship gate decides whether any candidate signal ships, and it is built to refute, not confirm. A signal is never tested in isolation; it must clear five criteria jointly -- an expanding walk-forward where every fold must improve, a null-shuffle permutation control the real effect must beat by at least three standard deviations, an ablation that measures the signal's marginal lift when added to the *full* production feature set rather than alone, a calibration and coverage check, and a closing-line-value check. A Benjamini-Hochberg correction runs across every signal ever tested to control false discovery, and a final held-out set is touched exactly once. If no leak-safe data bundle can be built, the gate returns DEFER -- never a false SHIP. That design is why the reject pile is so large: the gate was tuned to kill candidates, and it does.

Candidate ideas come from an LLM-free proposer that enumerates feature transforms from residuals and screens them with a cheap statistical filter, so discovery never runs out of hypotheses -- but the gate still decides, so volume never becomes noise.

Two guardrails are enforced in committed code, not politeness. A pre-edit check marks the production trees (the engine, the API) as protected, so an agent that tries to edit them is denied and routed to human review. An honesty linter blocks financial-performance language from any output, so an agent cannot ship an unsupported claim. These are the mechanical reason the fleet stays inside its lane while the human sleeps.

The system is also honest about its own size. It is roughly 430 Python modules, of which about 130 under the prediction folder are a research surface with only around a dozen load-bearing in the live deployment graph; the API layer serves about 99 endpoints across 12 routers. Being explicit that most of the surface is experiment, not production, is a judgment claim, not a size brag.

The current-era senior signal is not can you write code -- a fleet writes the code. It is whether you can direct that fleet so the output is trustworthy: route work by cost, run executors in parallel without corrupting the repo, and gate every result behind validation strict enough to reject your own favorite idea. The human wrote the gate, the guardrails, and the methodology; the agents wrote the implementation; and the split is recorded in git, not asserted.

essays.title: Reading an Entity Card Without Fooling Yourself
essays.dek: Every card names the floor that let it in and the thing it is not. Here is how to read one and not overreach.
essays.body_md:
The atlas renders one small analytics card per entity across every sport in the system -- 1,549 cards in total, 1,523 of them per-entity, each one traceable to a count you can reopen. Every card wears a red Descriptive only badge, a source-floor-as-of footer, and a descriptive-only flag. There is no forecast on these cards and no win probability. They show what an entity has done, gated by a declared minimum-sample floor, and nothing more. Reading one well is mostly a matter of respecting three things the card tells you about itself.

First, the floor. A card only exists if the entity cleared a stated inclusion threshold: an NBA player needs at least 800 career minutes (which admits 482 of 807 players), an MLB batter at least 300 pitches faced in 2025 (485 of 671), a tennis player at least 30 matches per surface, a soccer club at least 10 prior matches per metric. Below the floor the card shows n/a; it never fabricates a number to fill the gap. The floor is the first thing to read, because it tells you how much sample is under the pretty panel.

Second, what the rate is not. NBA player numbers are per-36-minute rates over a multi-season sample, not per-game and not opponent-adjusted. Jokic's 28.4 / 12.8 / 10.1 points, rebounds, and assists per 36 is a rate line, not a per-game average, and a per-36 triple-double is not a per-game one. The classic trap is a raw shooting percentage: Giannis shoots 60.9 percent from the field, which sounds like elite touch, but the range numbers give it away -- 27.4 percent from three, 64.0 percent at the line. The high field-goal mark is mostly about where the shots come from, a rim-heavy diet, which the raw percentage cannot separate from skill.

Third, and most dangerous, the confound. Two card families look like they measure individual value and do not. The team card's top contributor is simply the player with the most total minutes, not the best player: Boston's is Derrick White at 7,576.2 minutes and Golden State's is Brandin Podziemski at 6,018.4, not Curry. And the star-removal exhibit maps a team's on-off swing onto a win-probability curve, which reads dramatically -- Denver goes from 0.634 with Jokic to 0.0517 without, a 0.5822 swing -- but the card labels it a ceiling, not a clean player value, because it attributes a full-lineup on-versus-off gap to one man with no control for teammates, opponent, coach trust, or garbage time. The guardrail is in the same data: the median qualified player's on-off is just +0.127, so most such gaps are noise around zero, and the biggest on-off name on Boston is the role player Luke Kornet at 0.2785, not Tatum. A big on-off number is a flag to investigate, never a verdict.

The cards are served through the same fail-closed answer engine as everything else, so asking about an entity that was never built returns an honest no_data -- refusing, not guessing -- rather than a plausible invention. That is the whole design philosophy in miniature: wide coverage where every unit of it is individually auditable, down to the floor that let it in, and an explicit refusal the moment you reach past what the data supports. Read the floor, respect the rate, distrust the confound, and the card will not fool you.

essays.title: What the Ask AI Can and Cannot Tell You
essays.dek: It can only relay what the engine returns or admit it does not know. Three things it does well, three ways it refuses.
essays.body_md:
The Ask AI is not a chatbot improvising over some documents. It is a relay over a fail-closed engine. Every question routes to exactly one deterministic resolver chosen by rule, and the answer comes back as a typed envelope the model must honor verbatim: a status, the value, a sample size, a p-value, the exact source file, an as-of date, There is no room to round a number up, borrow a stale one, or invent an unsupported result. That structure is what lets it do three useful things and refuse three others honestly.

What it can do, tier one, is resolve a fact from a committed artifact -- a verified analytics claim, a calibration number, a descriptive entity card -- deterministically, the same number every time, because the same executable contract returns byte-identical results with no model call at all.

Tier two, it can return a mechanism receipt from the validation ledger. Ask whether the back-to-back rest penalty holds up in the NBA and it answers CONFIRMED_LOCAL with an effect of -1.73 points of margin, n=4,732, p about 0.0056, and the ledger file the finding lives in -- and the envelope's own framing field caps it at a local single-corpus finding, not a market-beating or causal claim. It confirms folklore and refuses to inflate it in the same breath.

Tier three, and the most telling, it can reprice a game in-game and tell on itself. Ask for a live NBA win probability at a given score and it returns the repriced number *and*, in the same envelope, the calibration for that game-state bucket: over 615 games, model Brier 0.2328 against market Brier 0.1985. The market is sharper in that spot, and the engine says so, out loud, unprompted. A system that reports its own losses against the benchmark is one you can trust when it reports a match.

What it cannot do is answer from thin air, and it refuses in three distinct ways rather than guessing. It returns no_data when the backing artifact is absent -- there is no live feed here, so tonight's odds, tonight's score, tomorrow's lineup, and any sport outside NBA, MLB, soccer, and tennis all come back as an honest no_data, not a borrowed number. It returns not_supported when no resolver is registered for the question type; the engine does not invent a handler. And it returns refused when the question requests financial guidance -- in the coverage stress test all 125 prohibited-language questions were refused, an ok-rate of exactly zero, enforced by the product rail rather than left to the model's discretion.

The honest part is that the gaps are measured and published, not hidden. Across a 1,307-question stress bank the status mix was 399 ok, 560 no_data, 42 not_supported, 181 ambiguous, and 125 refused, with zero errors, for an answerable-question coverage rate of 0.3662. Separately, a fail-closed regression bank runs 87 checks and passes all 87, where a correct no_data or not_supported counts as a pass. The design goal was never to answer everything. It was that a connected model cannot fabricate a number, and the honest gaps are visible and counted. That is the difference between an engine you can quote and a chat window that hopes.

essays.title: How to Read a Reliability Diagram
essays.dek: A reliability diagram compares what a probability said, on average, with what happened in the published group.
essays.body_md:
A reliability diagram is a compact audit of whether published probabilities mean what they appear to mean. It does not show individual games. It groups many recorded probability ticks into probability ranges, then asks two separate questions within each range: what was the average forecast, and how often did the terminal outcome occur? The horizontal position is the first number. The vertical position is the second. A point on the diagonal has equal values, so the average forecast and observed frequency agree for that bin. A point above the diagonal means the observed frequency was higher than the mean forecast. A point below it means the observed frequency was lower.

The page uses ten published ranges, from 0% to 10% through 90% to 100%. The range is an inclusion rule, not the displayed forecast. A point in the 0% to 10% range can sit at 5.12%, because 5.12% is the mean of the ticks assigned to that range. Its observed frequency can be 23.31%, because that is the terminal-outcome rate among those ticks. Reading the point as a single prediction would be a category error. It is a summary of a population of ticks.

The page also shows the signed gap in percentage points. It is observed frequency minus mean forecast, not a relative percentage change. In the published MLB model 0% to 10% bin, 23.31% minus 5.12% is +18.19 pp. The pp suffix matters. It says the difference is measured on the probability scale: 0.1819, expressed as 18.19 percentage points. It does not say that the observed frequency was 18.19 percent higher in a relative sense. Keeping those languages separate makes comparisons across bins legible.

That MLB example has 5,127 ticks from 133 games. The two counts are deliberately both visible. A tick is one recorded point on a probability path. A game can contribute many ticks, and nearby ticks from the same game commonly resemble one another. So 5,127 ticks describe the plotted population, while 133 games are the clustering units behind the uncertainty calculation. Neither number replaces the other. The chart is not claiming 5,127 independent games, and it does not turn the tick total into an invented independent-sample count.

The uncertainty bars make that distinction operational. The artifact records 1,000 bootstrap resamples, clustered by `game_id`, with a 2.5% to 97.5% interval. Resampling games as units preserves the fact that all ticks from a selected game travel together into that resample. The published MLB example has an observed-frequency interval from 15.49% to 32.39% and a gap interval from 10.40 pp to 27.38 pp. Those intervals describe variation under the stated resampling procedure; they are not a second estimate of the point itself.

Circle size is also a reading aid rather than a claim about independence. Larger circles correspond to more ticks in the selected view, and a hollow circle marks a bin the source flags as low n. The stated floor is at least five games per bin. That floor says which bins were eligible for display. It does not make every eligible bin equally precise, and it does not erase within-game dependence. Read the confidence interval, the game count, and the low-n flag together before assigning much weight to a point.

A useful pass through the page is therefore mechanical. Select a sport and series. Read the bin range, then the mean forecast and observed frequency. Subtract in the displayed direction to understand the pp gap. Check ticks and games separately. Finally, inspect the interval and low-n status before comparing that point with another one. The reliability diagram is not a verdict on every component of a forecasting system. It is a direct display of published agreement, or disagreement, between bin-level forecasts and outcomes.

The diagram also separates model and market series instead of combining them into one curve. Those are different published populations with their own ticks, game coverage, and bins. A reader should compare like with like: model against model across ranges, market against market across ranges, then the two series with their own support in view. The page's table keeps every published bin available precisely because a smooth line can hide the count and interval that give a plotted point its context.

essays.title: What a Brier Score Can and Cannot Tell You
essays.dek: The Brier score is a mean squared probability error. Its components help separate calibration from information concentration.
essays.body_md:
A Brier score is the mean squared difference between a probability and a 0 or 1 outcome. For one recorded tick, take the published probability, subtract the terminal outcome, and square the result. Average those squared errors across the published population. The score is on a probability-squared scale, and lower values indicate lower average squared error within the compared population. It is useful because it grades probability forecasts without choosing a single cutoff. It is not an accuracy percentage, a count of correct calls, or a measure of how often a forecast landed exactly on the outcome.

The score is broad by design. A low Brier score can arise from well-calibrated probabilities, from forecasts that sort situations into meaningfully different probability levels, or from both. A higher score can have several causes. That is why the page pairs the published score with a ten-bin Murphy decomposition rather than treating a single value as a diagnosis. The decomposition states the accounting relationship as Brier = reliability - resolution + uncertainty. Each term answers a different descriptive question.

Reliability is the component associated with gaps between bin-level mean forecasts and observed frequencies. Smaller reliability values indicate less of that measured mismatch in the binned reconstruction. Resolution captures how much the binned outcome frequencies differ from the population base rate; it is subtracted in the accounting identity. Uncertainty is the outcome variability in the population before conditioning on the forecast bins. It is a property of the observed population, not a quality label attached to one series. None of these terms alone is a complete explanation of a system.

The published MLB model row is a concrete worked example. It reports a Brier score of 0.237684 across 78,986 rows. Its binned reliability component is 0.012701, resolution is 0.023628, and uncertainty is 0.248092. Applying the stated identity to those three binned quantities gives 0.012701 - 0.023628 + 0.248092 = 0.237165. The artifact publishes the reconstructed value as 0.237166 after its own stored precision. The page then compares that reconstruction with the separately published Brier: 0.237166 - 0.237684 = -0.000518. That signed value is the reconstruction remainder.

The remainder is not an error the page silently removes. It is displayed because the reconstruction was computed from ten probability bins, while the published Brier is calculated from the original tick-level probabilities. Binning compresses a probability path into ten groups. That compression can change the arithmetic even when every input field is present. The page does not attribute a remainder to rounding, data quality, or a hidden adjustment unless the artifact publishes such a cause. It reports the signed difference and leaves the reason unassigned.

This distinction matters most when comparing rows. In the same MLB population, the published market row has Brier 0.206653, reliability 0.006061, resolution 0.047124, uncertainty 0.248092, and reconstructed Brier 0.207030. That row has a different reconstruction remainder from the model row because its binned distribution differs. The shared uncertainty does not make the rows interchangeable, and the score difference alone does not say which internal component should be changed. The decomposition gives a vocabulary for describing the published gap without turning it into a causal story.

A Brier score also cannot answer questions the artifact does not measure. It does not prove that a particular probability bin is well calibrated; use the reliability diagram for the bin-level values and intervals. It does not establish independence among repeated within-game ticks; use the observation-dependence page for the lag-1 residual distributions. It does not turn a descriptive snapshot into a current forecast. The population, series, and artifact date remain part of the measurement.

Read the decomposition table as an audit trail. Start with the published Brier. Read reliability, resolution, and uncertainty as the binned components used in the reconstruction. Then inspect the signed remainder instead of assuming the reconstruction must equal the unbinned score. This is more cautious than a one-number summary, and it preserves the line between an observed calculation and an explanation that has not been published.

essays.title: Why Repeated Ticks Are Not Repeated Evidence
essays.dek: Within a game, a smooth probability path can produce many ticks that carry closely related residual information.
essays.body_md:
A probability path can be recorded many times during one game. That creates a useful sequence for describing how the published forecast moved, but it does not create the same number of independent games. The observation-dependence page makes this visible with lag-1 residual autocorrelation: a comparison between each signed residual and the residual immediately before it within the same eligible game-side series. The residual is defined in the artifact as probability at time t minus the terminal outcome. The series are ordered by timestamp.

Lag-1 autocorrelation ranges from -1 to 1. A value near 1 means that consecutive residuals tend to move together. A value near 0 would indicate little linear relationship between adjacent residuals in that series. A negative value would indicate alternating movement. The page does not turn a high autocorrelation into a claim about forecast quality by itself. It describes dependence: how much one recorded residual resembles its neighbor in the same path.

The MLB model distribution provides a worked example. The artifact has 78,986 records across 227 candidate series. After its eligibility rules, 222 model series remain. Their median lag-1 residual autocorrelation is 0.9809, and 95.5% of eligible model series are above 0.9. In plain language, a 0.9809 median says adjacent residuals are extremely similar on the published linear autocorrelation measure. It does not say that 98.09% of predictions were correct, that the terminal outcome had a 98.09% frequency, or that one tick supplies 0.9809 of another tick's sample size. It is a property of the within-game residual sequence.

The structure of the data explains why this is plausible. The terminal outcome remains fixed for all ticks of a completed game, while a probability path often changes gradually from one timestamp to the next. Subtracting the same terminal value from a smooth path produces a smooth residual path. Many adjacent rows can therefore describe almost the same game state with only a small update between them. Treating every row as a fresh game would overstate how much distinct game-level evidence sits behind a calibration summary.

The page reports ticks and games separately because they answer different questions. The tick count tells the reader the size of the displayed recorded population. The eligible-series count tells the reader how many within-game series contributed to the autocorrelation distribution. The artifact applies a minimum of 10 rows per game and a minimum residual variance of 1e-9 before a series is eligible. In the MLB model population, two series were skipped for too few rows and three for flat residuals. Those exclusions are published rather than hidden inside the median.

It would be tempting to take the 0.9809 value, insert it into a formula, and declare a single effective sample size for every page. This site does not do that. An effective sample size depends on the estimand, the dependence structure beyond one lag, the weighting scheme, and the procedure that aggregates observations. One lag-1 summary is evidence of strong dependence, not a universal conversion from ticks to games. Publishing a precise-looking conversion without those ingredients would add an unsupported calculation.

The page keeps model and market arrays separate for the same reason. For MLB, the market series have median autocorrelation 0.9799 and 96.44% above 0.9 across 225 eligible series. Those are close published summaries, but they are still different populations with different skipped counts and paths. The dots are not paired observations. A comparison should preserve the side, sport, and eligibility context attached to the original value.

Use this page alongside the reliability diagram rather than in place of it. The reliability page reports bins, tick totals, game totals, and clustered bootstrap intervals. This page supplies the descriptive reason that repeated ticks deserve caution: the observed residual paths are highly serially related. Together, the pages make the counting rule visible without pretending that a single transformed count solves every inferential question.

essays.title: Reading an Atlas Analysis
essays.dek: An entity atlas is a committed collection of descriptive entity cards, not a single score or a current feed.

inspector.label: Open the MLB pitch type atlas analysis

essays.body_md:
An entity atlas is a published collection of entity-level records arranged so a reader can inspect the same committed measurements in several views. The atlas does not manufacture one universal ranking. It starts with the fields recorded for each entity, preserves the published units, and lets the reader select a field for a ranked list, scatter view, table, or distribution. The view changes the arrangement of the same measurements; it does not change what the fields mean.

The ranked view answers a narrow question: which published rows sort highest or lowest on the selected scalar field? That is useful for locating a record, but it is not a general quality judgment. A field such as median velocity and a field such as pitch share describe different things. Sorting a pitch-type share orders published usage frequency, while sorting `velo_p50` orders the middle recorded velocity. The selected field, its unit, and its cohort determine the interpretation.

The scatter view places two selected scalar fields on separate axes. It can show whether the published rows occupy a broad cloud, a narrow band, or a small cluster. It cannot establish that one field causes the other. The table is the audit-friendly alternative: it displays each row's available scalar fields, retains unavailable values as unavailable, and allows a reader to compare exact values. The distribution view shows the selected cohort spread and percentile ranks for the selected field. A percentile rank is within that field's available cohort, not a cross-field score.

The MLB pitch atlas illustrates the distinction. Its committed manifest contains 61 entries from a 2025 pull: 19 pitch types, 30 teams, and 12 count states. Each entry can carry scalar fields such as `n_pitches`, `pct_of_all_pitches`, and velocity percentiles, plus nested objects for count-state and outcome mixes. The derived atlas analysis intentionally ranks only finite scalar `key_numbers` fields. Nested objects remain on the entity card rather than being flattened into a misleading single measurement. This is a design choice that keeps a card's structured context intact.

Consider the pitch type CS. The manifest records 393 pitches, a median velocity of 72.4 mph, and `pct_of_all_pitches` of 0.06. That last field is already expressed as a percentage. The atlas field definition marks it as an already-percent value, so the analysis normalizes it for percent display without multiplying its meaning. The displayed result remains 0.06%, not 6% and not 0.0006%. Moving the decimal would turn a published frequency into a different measurement. The card and analysis preserve the source unit exactly.

Identifiers require similar care. `pitch_type:CS` is an identifier: it names the row. It is not a numerical measurement, so the atlas does not place it in the numeric cohort, assign it a percentile, or draw it as an axis value. Labels, card paths, and as-of dates identify provenance and navigation. They are vital context, but they are not competing measurements. Separating identifiers from scalars prevents a technically sortable field from being treated as an analytic one.

A percentile rank is therefore field-specific. If a reader selects `n_pitches`, the rank answers where a pitch type sits among available pitch-type rows by recorded count. If the reader then switches to `velo_p50`, the cohort is still the atlas's available pitch types, but the ordered variable has changed. One rank cannot be carried from the first field to the second. Missing or non-finite entries should remain outside the applicable numeric comparison rather than receiving an invented low rank.

The atlas also retains source floors and caveats. The MLB pitch manifest states that all 19 pitch-type codes in the 2025 pull are included and identifies the smallest category as n=7. That broad inclusion supports completeness of the manifest, not certainty that every small category is equally stable. A row with a small count can be displayed for completeness while still requiring cautious comparison. The field view and the source note belong together.

Read an atlas by choosing one concrete question. Select the relevant field, inspect its unit, then read the ranked, scatter, table, or distribution view as an arrangement of that field's published cohort. Open the entity card for nested measurements and the recorded floor. The result is a reproducible descriptive comparison, not a shortcut from an identifier to a conclusion.
cited: webapp/public/data/showcase/atlas_mlb_pitch_manifest.json -> entries[1].entity, key_numbers.n_pitches, key_numbers.pct_of_all_pitches, key_numbers.velo_p50, floors, as_of

essays.title: Calculation Inputs: How a Derived Row Is Reproduced
essays.dek: A derived row exposes its source paths and substituted operands so its displayed calculation can be checked against the committed artifact.
essays.body_md:
A derived analysis restates or calculates a value from a committed source artifact. The calculation-inputs panel is the receipt for one selected row. It lists the operands the analysis binds to that row, shows the source path for each operand, and displays the analysis formula with published values substituted when they are available. The goal is reproducibility: a reader should be able to see which source fields produced the displayed result without reconstructing the page's internal selection logic.

An operand binding has four parts. The operand is the symbol used in the formula. The source path says where that value came from in the source artifact. The value key says where the selected research row stores the published or derived value for display. The label gives the reader a human-readable name. The binding is not an extra data source. It is a declared link between the source artifact, the row, and the formula.

The comeback-rates analysis provides a direct worked example. Its selected row for Deficit 1-5 and 0-2 remaining comes from the source cell with `lead_band` `lead_+01_05` and `time_band` `rem_00_02`. That cell publishes `outcome_rate` 0.9865, `n_games` 344, `n_ticks` 21,297, and `masked_n_lt_30` false. The analysis labels the first two bands as Deficit 1-5 and 0-2 remaining, converts the rate to the leading-side outcome share, and retains the game and tick counts as support fields.

The displayed result uses the explicit formula: comeback share = 1 - outcome_rate. Substitution makes the calculation concrete: 1 - 0.9865 = 0.0135. The row displays that as a 1.35% observed comeback share because the research field formats the derived fraction as a percentage with two decimals. This is not a new source estimate. It is the complement of the published leading-side outcome rate, rounded only for presentation after the calculation is built. The companion 98.65% leading-side outcome share remains visible so the relationship can be checked in both directions.

The band labels are operands too, but they do different work from the numerical rate. `lead_band` and `time_band` identify which source cell the calculation uses. They do not enter the subtraction. `n_games` and `n_ticks` report support, but they are not denominators in this particular formula. `masked_n_lt_30` tells the reader whether the source marked the cell as small support. In this example it is false, so the cell clears the source's stated mask condition. The panel makes those roles separate instead of implying that every listed field is multiplied or divided.

The source path is intentionally literal. A path such as `cells[].outcome_rate` says the field lives on the selected object in the artifact's `cells` array. The brackets indicate an array member selected by the row, not an unqualified aggregate over every cell. The row's deficit and time bindings explain which member is in view. That distinction matters when many source cells share the same field name but represent different game states.

Sometimes the panel says `not published for this row`. That is a provenance status, not a zero and not a request to fill in a value. It means the analysis has a binding for a field, but the selected row lacks a finite number or nonempty string for that binding. The renderer preserves the missingness and leaves the general formula visible rather than substituting a made-up value. A reader can still inspect the source path, but should not infer that the unavailable operand equals zero or that another row's value applies.

The substituted equation appears only when all declared operands resolve. This protects against a formula that looks complete while silently omitting an input. When an operand cannot resolve, the page shows the original formula alongside the individual source paths. The source paths remain useful because they tell the reader what the analysis expected, even when the artifact did not publish enough to reproduce that particular row numerically.

Use calculation inputs as a boundary check. First verify the selected row's labels. Then compare each displayed operand with its source path. Read the substituted equation and confirm that the result field uses the stated unit. Finally, read the support counts and mask status before comparing it with another cell. The panel does not turn a descriptive row into a live estimate; it makes the published derivation inspectable.
cited: webapp/public/data/showcase/comeback_atlas.json -> cells[].lead_band, time_band, outcome_rate, n_games, n_ticks, masked_n_lt_30

essays.title: Reading a Score Decomposition Receipt
essays.dek: A worked score row keeps the published Brier value, its binned components, and the reconstruction remainder separate.
essays.body_md:
Start with one published row rather than comparing a headline score. The inspector places Brier, reliability, resolution, uncertainty, and the reconstructed score in the same receipt. Read the reconstruction remainder as the stated difference between the recorded score and the binned calculation. It is a check on the published arithmetic, not an assigned cause.

Then return to the reliability inspector for the bins that feed the decomposition. The two views answer different questions: one shows the grouped forecast-outcome gaps, while this receipt shows how the published components combine. Keep the sport, side, and snapshot attached to each row before comparing them.

essays.title: Reading Residual Anatomy by State
essays.dek: A state row reports recorded absolute error with its volume; it does not identify why that error occurred.
essays.body_md:
Choose one game-state row and read its recorded absolute residual beside the published row volume. That pairing distinguishes a large displayed error from a lightly represented state. The page preserves the state labels so a reader can identify the exact slice being described.

Before comparing state rows, open observation dependence. Repeated ticks inside a game can be closely related, so row volume is not interchangeable with independent game support. The inspector is a descriptive map of the recorded residuals, not a causal account of a forecast miss.

essays.title: Reading Blowout Timing
essays.dek: A permanent-margin table describes when a published game margin remained in place through the final clock.
essays.body_md:
Use the inspector as a sequence of observed conditions. First identify the permanent-margin definition in the source, then read the frequency and clock summaries for the displayed group. A margin that remains in place is a published retrospective condition, not a statement that a future lead is settled.

Read the comeback-rate analysis alongside this table. It keeps deficit and time remaining visible, which supplies the adjacent game-state context without turning either view into a causal threshold claim.

essays.title: Reading Adjacent State Contrasts
essays.dek: A contrast compares neighboring published state buckets while preserving the labels and support of both rows.
essays.body_md:
Select adjacent state buckets and read the published outcome-frequency difference with the source labels still in view. The contrast is a descriptive subtraction between recorded groups. It does not establish that crossing a boundary caused the outcome to change.

Use blowout timing first when the contrast concerns score and clock. That view makes the permanent-margin condition explicit, while the contrast view keeps the comparison local to the two published buckets.
